clue.text: Save thee, little ——': how doest thou, pretty rogue?" (Dekker, The Honest Whore)

definitions.text: Save thee, little ——': how doest thou, pretty rogue?" (Dekker, The Honest Whore)

parts.words: Save thee, little ——': how doest thou, pretty rogue?" (Dekker, The Honest Whore)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: the missing word is a small monkey that Dekker's speaker greets as a pretty rogue

explanation.surface: A line from a Jacobean comedy with one word blanked out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a literary quotation clue: the blank is filled by the word from the play, a pet name for a small tropical monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the Dekker line names a small South American monkey, used there as a teasing endearment.

clue.text: Mary McCarthy's leafy campus

parts.note: Mary McCarthy wrote the college novel The Groves of ..., and groves are leafy

explanation.surface: A remark about the tree-lined university setting of an American novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary McCarthy's 1952 novel is The Groves of Academe; 'leafy' points to the groves, and the campus is the world of scholarship itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the academic world, the university community, as in McCarthy's title.

clue.text: Location of Don Passos conveyance

parts.note: John Dos Passos wrote the novel ... Transfer, and a transfer is a conveyance; the place named is a New York borough

explanation.surface: A question about where a writer's vehicle can be found.
explanation.walkthrough: Dos Passos's 1925 novel is Manhattan Transfer; 'conveyance' stands for 'transfer', and the clue asks for the place in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The island borough of New York City is the setting named in the Dos Passos title.

clue.text: Sort of killer, of many parts?

explanation.surface: A question about a murderer who strikes repeatedly.
explanation.definitionFit: A repeat murderer is a serial killer, and a story issued in instalments is a serial, made of many parts.

clue.text: Bath featured in terminal scene for revolutionary journalist

definitions.text: Bath featured in terminal scene for revolutionary journalist

parts.words: Bath featured in terminal scene for revolutionary journalist
parts.note: Jacques-Louis David painted the French revolutionary journalist stabbed to death in his bath in 1793

explanation.surface: A description of a famous painting of a radical writer killed in his tub.
explanation.walkthrough: Marat, a journalist of the French Revolution, was murdered in his bath by Charlotte Corday; David's 1793 painting shows the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: David's painting depicts the murdered revolutionary slumped in his bathtub, the final scene of his life.

clue.text: Graceful swimmer covered with thanks in Bantu language

indicators.note: the bird is wrapped by the word for thanks, which covers it on both sides

parts.note: TA is informal British for thank you
a swan is the proverbially graceful bird on the water

explanation.surface: A swan is wrapped in gratitude while sitting in an African tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is a British informal 'thanks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Setswana is a Bantu tongue spoken in Botswana and South Africa.

clue.text: Schiller had a hand in it in 1797

definitions.text: Schiller had a hand in it in 1797

parts.words: Schiller had a hand in it in 1797
parts.note: Schiller's 1797 ballad Der Handschuh is named for a garment that a hand goes inside

explanation.surface: A remark that Schiller was involved in something in 1797.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had a hand in it' looks like 'was involved in'; read literally, a hand goes inside the thing, which is the title of Schiller's 1797 ballad Der Handschuh.
explanation.definitionFit: Schiller's ballad Der Handschuh translates into English as this title, a hand covering.

clue.text: Deceiver of biblical proportions

parts.note: in Acts 5 a man lies about the price of his land and is struck dead, so his name means a liar

explanation.surface: A description of a liar on an epic scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of biblical proportions' looks like 'enormous', but it means the deceiver comes from the Bible: in Acts he lied to the apostles.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Testament liar's name has passed into English as a byword for any habitual liar.

clue.text: He made the stage's best known hasty departure

definitions.text: He made the stage's best known hasty departure

parts.words: He made the stage's best known hasty departure
parts.note: in The Winter's Tale a courtier leaves the stage with the direction Exit, pursued by a bear

explanation.surface: A tribute to an actor who left the stage faster than anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's most famous stage direction, 'Exit, pursued by a bear', belongs to Antigonus in The Winter's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sicilian lord in The Winter's Tale flees from a bear, the stage's most famous exit.

clue.text: New rag reorchestrated for German musician

indicators.note: a piece reorchestrated is rearranged for new instruments, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ragtime tune rearranged for a German composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorchestrated' rearranges NEWRAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Wagner was the German composer of the Ring cycle.

clue.text: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?

definitions.text: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?

parts.words: Smith recorded his song, accompanied by trumpets?
parts.note: the singer whose song is accompanied by trumpeting is a large tusked animal, since its call is called a trumpet

explanation.surface: A singer named Smith made a record backed by a brass section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumpets' suggests a brass band, but it is the call of the animal whose song was recorded.
explanation.definitionFit: The big African or Asian beast with a trunk makes a trumpeting call, the sound the clue describes.

clue.text: Hope's development is thus distinct

explanation.surface: A claim that Hope's progress has made something stand apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Hope, a South African novelist, wrote A Separate Development (1980), whose title echoes the apartheid euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Hope's novel is A Separate Development, and the adjective also means apart or not joined.

clue.text: Novel affection of Henry Vincent Yorke

definitions.text: Novel affection of Henry Vincent Yorke

parts.words: Novel affection of Henry Vincent Yorke
parts.note: Henry Vincent Yorke wrote under the name Henry Green, and one of his novels has a title meaning fondness

explanation.surface: A remark about a man's new attachment.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Vincent Yorke published as Henry Green; his 1945 novel is Loving. 'Novel' reads as 'new' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Green's 1945 novel has a one-word title that also means showing affection.

clue.text: Poet takes skate or steak for a change

indicators.note: the letters of the word are changed round into a new order

explanation.surface: A poet orders fish instead of beef just for variety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes', 'skate' and 'steak' are all anagrams of the poet; 'for a change' rearranges STEAK.
explanation.definitionFit: John Keats was the English Romantic poet of the great odes.

clue.text: Forcibly removed from 14

explanation.surface: Someone was taken by force from somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 across is the author; this is his 1886 novel about David Balfour, who is abducted.
explanation.definitionFit: Abducted by force; also the title of the 1886 adventure novel by the author at 14 across.

clue.text: His fellow-traveller was an ass

parts.note: Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes is by the Scottish writer whose companion was a donkey called Modestine

explanation.surface: An insult to someone's travelling companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ass' looks like a slur on a friend, but it is literal: the writer walked the Cevennes in 1878 with the donkey Modestine.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Travels with a Donkey about his walk with Modestine.

clue.text: According to Williams play, it's inevitable

definitions.text: According to Williams play, it's inevitable

parts.words: According to Williams play, it's inevitable
parts.note: Emlyn Williams wrote the thriller Night Must Fall, so the coming of dark is a must

explanation.surface: A claim that a Williams drama predicts something unavoidable.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Tennessee: Emlyn Williams's 1935 thriller Night Must Fall says the evening's dark is inevitable.
explanation.definitionFit: Emlyn Williams's title says the onset of dark must come, so it is inevitable.

clue.text: Strains occasioned by a lot of poetry

definitions.text: occasioned by a lot of poetry

explanation.surface: Tensions that arise from reading too much verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Strains are pressures or tensions, and metrical verse is built from accented syllables.

clue.text: Terminal fate a game to Barker

explanation.surface: A dying fate treated as sport by someone named Barker.
explanation.walkthrough: Clive Barker's first novel was The Damnation Game (1985).
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal punishment in hell is the final fate, and Clive Barker's horror novel is The Damnation Game.

clue.text: Drayton's the Faire, seen as brilliant child by Dahl

explanation.surface: A fair lady in an old poem reappears as a gifted girl in a children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Drayton wrote the poem Matilda the Faire and Chaste Daughter (1594); Roald Dahl's heroine is a child genius.
explanation.definitionFit: Drayton's 1594 poem is titled after the fair and chaste heroine, and Dahl's gifted girl has the same name.

clue.text: Eponymous saint of 13 Across

parts.note: the poet at 13 across wrote The Eve of St ..., a narrative poem named after a virgin martyr

explanation.surface: A question about a saint who gives her name to a poet's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 across's poem The Eve of St Agnes takes its title from the saint whose feast falls on 21 January.
explanation.definitionFit: The virgin martyr whose eve is celebrated gives her name to the poem's title.

clue.text: It comes halfway between two Miller works

definitions.text: It comes halfway between two Miller works

parts.words: It comes halfway between two Miller works
parts.note: Henry Miller wrote Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, and the line midway between the tropics circles the earth

explanation.surface: Something placed midway between two of a writer's books on a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Miller, not Arthur: his Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn name the two tropics, and the line midway between them is the clue's answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The great circle of zero latitude lies halfway between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

clue.text: Source of higher education that French find singular

parts.note: a uni, short for university, is where higher education comes from
que is French for that

explanation.surface: French people find a university place unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: UNI is informal for university.
explanation.definitionFit: Something one of a kind is singular in the sense of extraordinary.

clue.text: It makes an offer that cannot be declined

definitions.text: It makes an offer that cannot be declined

parts.words: It makes an offer that cannot be declined
parts.note: in grammar a noun that cannot be declined has no case endings; the clue echoes the Godfather's offer he can't refuse

explanation.surface: A Mafia-style proposal that nobody is allowed to turn down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declined' means refused in the surface, but in grammar a noun declined takes case endings; the answer is a noun with no inflections.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, a noun lacking any case forms is indeclinable, which is what this term names.

clue.text: I rout man " might be suggested by monster. Or is this a lot of bull?

indicators.note: the phrase's letters, mixed up, suggest the name of the creature

explanation.surface: A monster prompts a fighting cry, or perhaps it is all nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I rout man' rearranged spells the beast of Crete; 'a lot of bull' is a pun on its half-bull form.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cretan beast, half man and half bull, lived in the labyrinth.

clue.text: Plantagenet politician

parts.note: Plantagenet is a first name here: Trollope's Plantagenet ..., later Duke of Omnium, becomes Prime Minister

explanation.surface: A medieval royal who went into politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plantagenet' looks like the royal house, but it is the first name of Trollope's statesman, hero of The Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's Plantagenet, Duke of Omnium, is the statesman of his political novels.

clue.text: Large bottle of whisky given with love for eight pages

parts.note: a quart is a large measure, two pints of drink
love means nil in tennis, so the round letter O

explanation.surface: A big whisky bottle is a gift of affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is zero in tennis, so O.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheet folded twice gives four leaves, that is eight pages, the book format so named.

clue.text: Tot so presented on stage

parts.note: a tot is a small drink, as is a dram
as and so both mean in the way stated

explanation.surface: A child is presented in a school play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a small child; it is a small measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Plays are works performed in a theatre.

clue.text: Splendour of Edward Thomas

explanation.surface: Praise for a Welsh-English poet's magnificence.
explanation.definitionFit: Glory is magnificence, and Edward Thomas wrote a poem with this title about morning beauty.
